extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students (patent litigation practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the allocation of questions of law and fact in patent litigation, and on how courts should construe specifications and claims (including when to rely on evidence, the state of the art, and jury findings). Focuses on novelty/identity, utility, claim scope, and use of extrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/identity based on evidence in pais is for the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant alleges the plaintiff's invention was in public use or substantially contained in a printed publication (i.e., where identity is in dispute and supported by evidence in pais), the issue of novelty and identity is to be left to the jury under proper instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court's role is to instruct the jury as to what constitutes novelty and sufficiency of invention; the weighing of evidence of prior public use or publication (identity disputes) is a jury question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court constructs written instruments (specifications and claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction (legal meaning) of a specification or claim, as a written instrument, belongs to the court; the court must determine, upon the whole instrument, what the claim actually covers and whether the patent is valid in point of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The jury must take the construction of the patent (as to extent of claim) from the court and apply it to determine novelty. If the specification is ambiguous such that meaning cannot be ascertained, the law may declare it insufficient for uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: When technical terms require evidence, meanings are matters of fact for the jury
rubrics_metrics.description: Although construction belongs to the court, where a specification contains technical terms, phrases of art, or descriptions that require explanation by evidence (surrounding circumstances, state of the art, proof of results, chemical equivalents), the explanation of such terms and the factual meaning of the description are matters of fact upon which evidence may be given and which the jury may decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court should give legal exposition of the document taken independently; after that, comparing whether interpreted words denote the same external matter is a factual inquiry for the jury and the court's instructions may be conditional upon jury findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of two specifications: identity often a jury question
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two specifications employ terms of art or technical language, the court cannot, merely by comparing the documents, pronounce the inventions identical; identity of signification between two documents describing external things is generally a matter of evidence for the jury, not solely of construction by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even identical language in two specifications does not guarantee they denote the same external object unless it is ascertained (by evidence) that the terms had the same signification at the dates of the respective specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee may forfeit protection by improper claim wording
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who actually invented a useful machine or process may still lose the patent (in whole or in part) if the claim is so clumsily drawn as to comprise matters of which the patentee is not the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury findings as to who invented what do not save a patent whose claim on its face covers things beyond the patentee's invention; the court must pronounce such a patent invalid to the extent it claims more than the inventor's actual invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewed patent same-invention and abandonment are factual questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a renewed patent is for the same invention as the original, and whether an invention has been abandoned to the public, are questions of fact for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence about acts, acquiescence, and the circumstances controls these factual determinations, though the court may state legal conclusions where all facts are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility: legal vs factual components
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of utility has two aspects: (1) whether the subject-matter is injurious or against public policy (not a patentable subject) — this is a question of law for the court; (2) whether the means asserted to achieve an innocuous object actually will succeed in practice — this depends on evidence and is a question of fact for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is enough for validity that an invention is capable of some use; total failure of an essential claimed element renders the patent invalid as a factual matter. The degree or extent of usefulness is immaterial if the invention is capable of some use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frivolous or insignificant objects are questions of law
rubrics_metrics.description: If the object proposed to be accomplished by the invention is frivolous or insignificant from which no advantage can be derived to the public, the patent is void as not being for a patentable subject — a legal determination for the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If object is not clearly frivolous but the means fail to produce result, the issue reverts to factual inquiries about usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court must decide ambiguity/uncertainty of specification as a legal question
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a specification is ambiguous and therefore insufficient is generally a question of law to be decided by the court; the court cannot improperly leave the legal question of ambiguity to the jury by making such determination conditional on jury findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where meaning cannot be ascertained satisfactorily on the face of the specification, the court should either rule the patent void for uncertainty or decide its meaning and direct the jury accordingly (see Emerson v. Hogg example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the descriptive parts of the specification to construe the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Resort may be had to the descriptive parts of the specification (preamble, body, summing up) to ascertain what the patentee has said he has invented; the court should, if possible and without violating principle, construe the claim so as to include the actual invention previously set forth (ut res magis valeat quam pereat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the whole instrument together unless the summary explicitly excludes part of the description. The real invention is an auxiliary to the construction of the language employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where descriptive terms leave doubt, look to evidence of the state of the art and actual invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If the precise extent of the invention is uncertain from the description alone (but not so ambiguous as to be void), the court must attend to evidence showing what is new or old, the state of the art, and whether the patentee discovered the underlying principle or only a particular form of application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether patentee claimed a general application of a principle (entitling broader claims) or only a particular form; this inquiry involves assessing substance and essence of the invention from evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge may receive and use evidence of actual invention when construing the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: In the course of trial the judge should inform himself from the evidence about the state of the art and the surrounding circumstances bearing on the meaning of the claim; if the material facts are not in doubt, construction will be given absolutely, but if evidence requires findings by the jury, the court's construction may be conditional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge 'must gather as he goes along' — observe which facts are controverted — and apply the appropriate legal construction either absolutely or conditionally depending on whether factual determinations remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that patentee does not intend to claim known matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is to be presumed not to intend to claim things which he must know to be in use; a specification should be read, consistently with fair import of language, so as to make the claim coextensive with the actual discovery or invention and not to include matter known before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The previous existence, familiarity, and constant use of something mentioned in the specification are elements in deciding whether the patentee intended to claim it as his own invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art limits the interpretation of general terms (ejusdem generis)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent contemplates use of certain substances and uses general terms broad enough to embrace others, those general terms will be interpreted to include only substances ejusdem generis with the particular substances mentioned which may reasonably have been contemplated at the time, ascertained by evidence of the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General language should be read in light of what would reasonably have been contemplated on the state of the art at the patent's date (e.g., excluding later-discovered substitutes not reasonably foreseeable or economically practical at the time).
